graphic.alt-text: Flowchart illustrating blood and fluid intake and output indicators in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), heart failure, and subsequent multiple organ failure (MOF), showing laboratory values, fluid treatments, and clinical events at key time points, recommending sodium bicarbonate infusion and a switch to 5 percent glucose injection when blood glucose is under thirteen point nine millimoles per liter.

caption.p: Schematic diagram of mechanisms. This diagram illustrates a hypothetical mechanism by which three core pathophysiological processes interact to cause refractory mixed acidosis and subsequent multiorgan dysfunction. Left panel (Peripheral metabolic pool hypothesis): In severe DKA states, insufficient peripheral tissue perfusion leads to the accumulation of ketones (particularly β-hydroxybutyrate) and lactate in peripheral tissues, forming a “peripheral metabolic pool.” Following fluid resuscitation and insulin therapy, central circulating glucose and ketone levels decline, while restored peripheral perfusion “washes back” these sequestered acidic metabolites into the central circulation, causing transient or persistent aggravation of acidosis—a mechanism analogous to ischemia-reperfusion injury. Right panel (Hypothesized mechanisms of iatrogenic hyperchloremic acidosis): Massive infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride, combined with acute kidney injury (AKI, serum creatinine from 34 to 302.9 μmol/L), leads to impaired chloride excretion and progressive hyperchloremia (serum Cl- from 96.77 to 115 mmol/L). This results in hyperchloremic normal anion gap acidosis, which superimposes on the original high anion gap ketoacidosis, forming a mixed severe acidosis (Δ gap=ΔAG-ΔHCO3 - = -15). Bottom panel (end-organ effects): The mixed acidosis further triggers: (1) cardiac contractility depression and myocardial energy metabolism impairment, leading to acute heart failure (NT-proBNP 8709 pg/mL); (2) lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity inhibition and aggravated insulin resistance, exacerbating hypertriglyceridemia; and (3) glomerular afferent arteriole vasoconstriction, along with glomerular and tubular injury, resulting in AKI. Reduced proximal tubular HCO3 - reabsorption (urine β2-microglobulin >4000 μg/L, serum β2-MG 8166.71 μg/L) further amplifies the acid load. DKA, diabetic ketoacidosis; LPL, lipoprotein lipase; AKI, acute kidney injury; CRRT, continuous renal replacement therapy.

graphic.alt-text: Diagram illustrates the pathophysiology of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) following massive sodium chloride infusion, showing peripheral metabolic and nephron hypotheses. Arrows trace mixed acidosis, severe acidosis, and related complications: hyperchloremic acidosis, impaired glomerular filtration, reduced bicarbonate reabsorption, increased ketones, impaired cardiac function, increased triglycerides, and risk of acute kidney injury.
